episodes.215862: August started off on an active note, with several rounds of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area. This stemmed from a low pressure system that ushered a warm front into West Virginia on August 2nd, maintaining a warm and unsettled environment for storms to thrive. The bulk of activity wound down during the evening, however some additional storms accompanied a cold front that swept through the area that night. The front stalled just east of the Appalachian Mountains on the 3rd, allowing isolated to scattered showers to linger over eastern West Virginia for much of the day. ||Storms featured during this timeframe were strong enough to produce damaging wind gusts that brought down trees and power lines. Storm damage was mainly observed in the foothills of the state, including Braxton, Clay, Webster, and Fayette Counties. A good portion of West Virginia received around an inch of rain, with pockets of two to three inch accumulations in central and southeast parts of the state. The highest 72-hour rainfall amounts, ranging from three to four inches, accrued in eastern Raleigh and Fayette Counties. This led to flooding on several roads.

episodes.217749: A slow-moving cold front approaching from the west and a warm front lifting northward led to a moisture-rich environment along with modest instability. As a result, locally heavy showers and isolated thunderstorms, especially during the afternoon and at night, led to isolated instances of roadway flooding and the flooding of a few basements.

episodes.218147: On August 2nd, 2026, the Weather Prediction Center placed Western New York under a Marginal Excessive Rainfall Outlook as a tropical-moisture-rich environment interacted with an incoming slow-moving boundary. Area Forecast Discussions from NWS Buffalo emphasized unseasonably high precipitable water values, warning that repeated rounds of heavy showers and thunderstorms could produce intense rainfall rates exceeding two inches per hour. A widespread Flood Watch was hoisted across all of Western New York, and multiple Flash Flood Warnings were subsequently issued by late afternoon and evening as convective storms trained across the region, including north-central Erie County. The resulting downpours led to rapid urban runoff, road inundations, and localized flash flooding across vulnerable low-lying infrastructure throughout the metro area.
episodes.218329: An upper high over the southwest and a disturbance moving through northeast flow triggered thunderstorms over the Gila region where severe hail fell and the storms moved southwest onto the Lordsburg Playa bringing wind gusts over 60 mph and a dust storm.
episodes.218344: Scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms developed along an inverted trough that extended across western and into central North Dakota early in the morning. Elevated storms managed to mix down a few isolated damaging severe wind gusts. The strongest measured gust was 66 mph at the Huff Hills mesonet station. Scattered downed tree branches were reported across the Bismarck/Mandan area.
episodes.218418: An active monsoon day brought severe thunderstorms across portions of Southeastern Arizona that caused numerous trees to be damaged or uprooted, recorded wind gusts ranging from 58 to 88 mph, damage to roofs and homes, downed power lines that caused power outages, and 1 inch diameter hail. Additionally, there was flash flooding due to locally heavy rainfall from thunderstorms that caused roadways to become impassable.

episodes.218487: On August 3rd a pre-frontal trough and weak jet streak moved across the state.  This upper level feature was aided by moderate low level moisture and daytime heating to help trigger thunderstorm development across Northern New Hampshire.  Enough shear and terrain enhancements allowed a few storms to become severe with localized damaging wind gusts.  In addition, during the morning, a moist airmass and stalled boundary triggered heavy rain over Southern New Hampshire, with caused excessive rainfall and urban flooding in Nashua.
episodes.218587: A convective cloud line developed along the Florida Bay and Gulf of America side of the Middle Florida Keys.  A waterspout was observed near Long Key.
episodes.218588: An outflow boundary originating from strong thunderstorms north of Cuba propagated northward, focusing new thunderstorm development moving north through the Lower Florida Keys.  Scattered gale-force wind gusts and several waterspouts were observed.

events.narrative: A NWS meteorologist, a Naval Air Station Key West weather observer and members of the public observed multiple waterspouts southeast of Key West and Stock Island.  All three waterspouts had full condensation clouds that extended from cloud base to the water surface with visible spray rings.  The westernmost waterspout was mostly vertical and of medium width.  The central waterspout was oriented at a 45-degree angle and of medium width.  The easternmost waterspout, observed from the Naval Air Station Key West at Boca Chica Key, was mostly vertical about three-quarters of the way up from the surface, then made a sharp angle to the parent cloud base at an approximately 60 degree angle.  The easternmost waterspout was also of the widest width.  Movement of the waterspouts was estimated toward the west at 5 to 10 knots, with the family of waterspouts lasting at least over a 30-minute duration.
